analysis.title: US Election Monitor: Final Update and What to Watch Tonight
key_insights: Prediction markets implied over a 70% chance Democrats win the Senate as of November 2, up from roughly 60% two weeks earlier. They imply over 90% for a Democratic House win.
Democratic candidates lead polls in all the Senate seats they hold plus 7 Republican-held seats. The marginal races are within the margin of error.
Polling errors in recent midterm Senate elections have been polarized, with Republicans outperforming final preelection polls in red states such as Alaska, Ohio and Texas.

Early voting share leans more Democratic than in 2024 in all key Senate states, including Texas. The party turnout gap looks smaller among NYT/Siena respondents who are 'almost certain' to vote, because Democrats vote earlier and Republicans vote disproportionately on election day.

Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot by an average of 8.9pp. That implies an 11-12pp swing from the 2.6pp national popular vote margin by which House Republicans won in 2024. The Democratic lead has changed little over recent weeks.

Republicans hold about 30 districts that Trump won by less than 11pp. If Republicans win every seat where prediction markets favor them, Democrats would net about 25 seats for a total of 240 next year.
GS believes a Democratic House win matters more to the policy outlook than the Senate outcome.

KY-06 (R+15 in 2024, polls close 6:00 PM ET) is an early signal. Democrat Dembo coming within a few points would suggest Democrats are having as good an election as polls suggest. Counting is slow, and early returns lean Democratic because of pre-Election Day votes.

FL-14 (Trump +10.5pp, redrawn) resembles the 11pp national shift and looks demographically similar to Texas. Rep. Castor (D) led by 5pp in a recent Emerson poll, and a Democratic loss would suggest polls overstated Democratic support.

NC-1 was redrawn to a Trump +11.5pp district and is seen as a toss-up. A win by incumbent Democrat Don Davis would suggest Democrats are performing in line with polls. Roy Cooper is very likely to win the NC Senate race, leading polls by 11-12%, but North Carolina's strong Democratic early vote limits the read-across to IA, KS, MI, OH and TX.

OH-Senate polls close at 7:30 PM ET, with 90% of votes expected counted by 10:30 PM. It could be the earliest marginal Senate race called. A Democratic loss in Ohio plus underperformance in Texas would make a Democratic Senate majority unlikely, since Democrats would then also need Alaska, Maine, Iowa and North Carolina.

VA-01, VA-02 and VA-05 give a read on the size of the Democratic House majority by 10:30 PM. VA-02 tests whether Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) can survive a national Democratic shift, which also bears on Collins in Maine and Hinson in Iowa.

TX-Senate: most polls close at 8:00 PM ET and over half the vote should be counted within an hour. Early counts will likely lean several points more Democratic than the final result, since remaining Election Day voters lean Republican. A tight race may not be called until late at night or the next morning.
Michigan and Maine are unlikely to be called before Wednesday. Alaska could take several days if the race is tight because of ranked choice voting.
risk_factors: Marginal Senate races are within the polling margin of error.
Polling errors have become more polarized in recent midterm Senate elections, with Republicans outperforming final polls in red states.
Early counts in Texas will likely lean several points more Democratic than the final result.
Close races in Texas, Michigan, Maine and Alaska may take days to call, delaying clarity on Senate control.

tension_points.bull_case: Prediction markets imply over a 70% chance of a Democratic Senate, up from roughly 60% two weeks earlier. Democrats lead polls in all their own seats plus 7 Republican-held seats.
tension_points.bear_case: The marginal races are within the margin of error. Republicans have outperformed final polls in red states such as Alaska, Ohio and Texas in recent midterms.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Democratic loss in Ohio combined with underperformance in Texas would make a Democratic Senate majority unlikely.
